Caravaggio. The Italian Baroque painter celebrated for his dramatic use of chiaroscuro—violent contrasts between deep shadows and vivid light—and his unflinching realism that brought sacred subjects into ordinary taverns and streets. His revolutionary technique and turbulent life made him foundational to Baroque art, though his violent temperament left him perpetually at odds with patrons and the law.

Caravaggio pioneered chiaroscuro to create psychological intensity and direct emotional force in religious scenes, influencing nearly every Baroque painter who followed. He painted The Calling of Saint Matthew in a tavern, depicting Christ entering a dive bar to summon a tax collector. Sacred narrative rendered in grimy, lived-in reality. The Conversion of Saint Paul and Saint Peter's Crucifixion present martyrdom from shocking, undignified angles. He was commissioned to paint altarpieces that shocked rather than consoled.

His Judith Beheading Holofernes gives the biblical widow an urgent, muscular physicality. It is often considered a self-portrait of moral ambiguity. In 1606, he fled Rome after killing a man in a brawl. He spent his final years in Naples, Malta, and Sicily, painting while evading capture. His style grew darker and more anguished.

Caravaggio worked directly on canvas with minimal preparation, painting wet-on-wet, making revisions rare and execution visible. A method that impressed and unsettled his peers. He died young, around thirty-seven, in obscurity on a beach, possibly of malaria or infected wounds. Nearly forgotten until scholars rediscovered his influence in the twentieth century. His innovations made him the blueprint for Baroque intensity and realism across Europe.
